text: This is a car reversing in India.
Not beeping. Performing.
An engineer designed a little beep, so you'd know a car was behind you. India heard that and thought: what if it was also a wedding band?
This one doesn't beep. It plays a full Bollywood song. Every time it backs out of the parking. Twice a day. For three years.
It is the one sound on an Indian road that makes everyone stop. Not to make way. To hear the chorus.
Abroad, a horn means one thing. "Danger."
Here, the horn is a language. And like every Indian language, it has dialects.
One short beep: "I'm here." Two short beeps: "I'm passing." Three: "I'm passing, and I want you to know I was patient."
One long horn: "I have opinions about your driving." One very long horn: "I have opinions about your family."
And a horn at a red light, with nobody moving anywhere: that one is not for anyone. That one is a feeling.
The Hero Splendor. The most common bike in the country. Unwashed, unkillable. Its natural load: a man, his wife, two children, a gas cylinder, and a goat that has agreed to the arrangement.
Field note: the real backbone of the country. Has never been serviced. Has never needed to be.
She's turning left.
The Activa. Rider: often an aunty, dupatta tied over her face like a very polite bank robber. The left indicator has been on since the monsoon. Nobody tells her.
Two kilometres. Three flyovers. Still left.
The Royal Enfield. Habitat: Instagram. Call: thump, thump, thump, and a pop that frightens a cow. Every rider is going to Ladakh next year. Since 2017.
He wears a leather jacket in May. He calls this "the vibe."
This year, though? This year, for sure.
The KTM. Habitat: the gap that doesn't exist. Call: braap, braap, at a red light, going nowhere. The rider is nineteen, with one orange stripe. Every ride is a reel.
Light's green. Gap? Still no gap.
Mumbai's police once wired a few signals to a sound meter. If the honking at a red light got too loud, the timer went back to ninety. "Honk more, wait more."
The only traffic rule ever enforced by peer pressure. It worked.
And the most famous three words on Indian roads. Horn. OK. Please.
Nobody knows why it says "OK." There are three theories. Every truck driver believes a different one, completely.
The Maharashtra government once tried to ban it, to cut down on honking. The trucks kept painting it on.
It's the only vehicle on the road that writes down its rules. It also follows them.
"Bhaiya, main road kaise jaayein?"
The driver points with his chin. A chin can give very precise directions. "Seedha. Petrol pump se left. Phir mandir ke baad, jahan pehle bargad ka ped tha, wahan se right."
Where the banyan tree used to be. It isn't there anymore. Everyone still uses it.
"Google pe toh..."
"Google ko kya pata, sir."
Every morning, Rohit's drive turns into a video game. Three lives. One car. No save points.
He knows every pothole by heart. The one outside the bank. The one that ate his silencer. And a new one, since Tuesday. He lost a life.
Two lives left. Same road home tonight.
He lives eleven kilometres from his office. Google Maps says twenty-six minutes. Google Maps says this every morning. Google Maps has never driven here.
Field note: distance in India is not measured in kilometres. It is measured in "depends."
Rohit reached the office at nine forty-one. Sixty-one minutes. Google Maps said twenty-six. For the drive home, Google Maps is already saying twenty-six.
Rule one. Stay in your lane.
Three lanes. Five rows of traffic. The paint is not a rule. It's a suggestion, made by a man with a brush, who has since retired.
Field note: a lane is not where you drive. It is where you started.
